fields.expected: The work I keep coming back to is where agents meet real users and real failure modes, which is exactly what Sierra is doing with customer experiences for companies like Uber, CLEAR, and Sutter Health. When I built a Playwright job-application agent in TypeScript, the hard part was not making the browser act. It was deciding where automation should stop. I put every application through an explicit state machine with SQLite as the single source of truth, gated every mutating capability behind fail-closed flags, and architecturally prevented free-text essay and demographic fields from being auto-filled. I also built a validation ladder from unit fixtures up to live mutation so a capability was never called working just because it passed locally. That instinct came partly from Intelehealth, where I evaluated LLM-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case standard and learned that generating an answer is cheap while deciding whether to trust it is not. Sierra is deploying agents where a wrong action reaches an actual customer, so evaluation and reliability are not side concerns. I also want to work somewhere in person where interns own real pieces of a system, and where craftsmanship is stated as a value rather than assumed.

fields.expected: The agent engineers I'd trust are the ones who treat evaluation as the real engineering problem. Getting an LLM to produce an action is cheap. Deciding whether that action should be trusted, and what happens when it is wrong, is where the work is. At Intelehealth I designed an evaluation framework for AI-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case benchmark, using stratified sampling to surface systematic failure modes rather than reporting a single accuracy number. That changed how I build agents. In my job-application agent I added a validation ladder, UNIT_CONFIRMED to FIXTURE_CONFIRMED to LIVE_READ_ONLY_CONFIRMED to LIVE_MUTATION_CONFIRMED, because a capability passing against a local fixture is not the same as it working against reality. In tSearch, I kept discovery separate from LLM judging so the judges could not silently paper over identity-resolution errors, and made missing evidence return "insufficient evidence" instead of a low score. I also ship: ClarityAtlas went into a live Hopkins pilot with 30+ users, and SnapSort reached 300+. I am an undergraduate, not a senior engineer, but I have built agent systems end to end and I care about where automation should stop.

fields.expected:
Two things that did not fit elsewhere. First, I do product work as well as engineering. I co-founded Open Health Intelligence and led the build of ClarityAtlas, an iOS app in Swift and SwiftUI with a passive sleep-estimation system using HealthKit and Core Motion signals so users would not need a wearable. We shipped it into a live pilot at Hopkins with 30+ users, got into the Pava Spark Accelerator and NSF I-Corps, and received a non-binding indication of about $75,000 for 7 to 8 percent that we chose not to take because the partnership was not the right one. Recruiting users and explaining why the thing should exist took as much work as writing it.

Second, I have spent the past year independently studying how research gets funded and evaluated, interviewing researchers, administrators, and science-policy people. The conclusion I keep landing on is that as AI makes generation cheap, judgment becomes the bottleneck. That is the same reason agent reliability interests me.

I'm an undergrad at Johns Hopkins in Applied Math and Statistics and Economics, class of 2029.
